newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Peru hostages learn to live under the gun.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Peru hostages learn to live under the gun.

text.p: No one has seen them in public for more than three months except for a few fleeting glimpses through a window or on a rooftop. But they are Peru's most talked-about people.

The 72 hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's residence may be pawns in a struggle of wills between the Marxist rebels holding them and President Alberto Fujimori's government, but as talks to end the standoff crawl ahead concern has grown in Peru about their physical and mental health.

"These people started with panic and then moved to mere terror and from there to something like daily fear, the kind of fear you learn to live with every day," said Hector Jhon Caro, a former chief of Peru's anti-terrorism police.
"They live and breathe and sleep in uncertainty about their lives," said Jhon Caro, who has dealt with people kidnapped for ransom by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
The 72 men -- the women were all released long ago -- include an all-star list of cabinet ministers, ambassadors, diplomats and businessmen, and Fujimori's brother.

The only thing they have in common is that all went to a cocktail party hosted by the Japanese ambassador on Dec. 17 and were taken hostage along with more than 400 others when MRTA rebels overran the place with bombs and sub-machineguns. The guerrillas released the other hostages but kept the most valuable bargaining chips to trade for the release of about 450 of their comrades from jail, their main demand.
LITTLE KNOWN ABOUT THEIR DAILY LIVES

What little is known about the hostages' lives in captivity comes from doctors who accompany Red Cross staff into the mansion to treat their medical ailments and from letters the hostages send to relatives outside. They describe a weirdly quiet life in which hostages spend 12 hours a day sleeping and rarely move around, living constantly under the guns of their captors who have explosives strapped to their torsos, ready to blow the whole place sky-high if police try anything funny.

"I think they've gotten over the panic stage," said one of the doctors, who asked not to be identified. "They rest a lot. There is no electricity in the house so they go to bed (early) ... or they read by candlelight."

None of the hostages seemed depressed, the doctor said. They get fresh air daily in a garden behind the home, out of the view of reporters stationed in apartment towers a block away, and they all cooperate on daily tasks from sweeping floors to cleaning toilets. "It doesn't matter if you're an ambassador or a millionaire businessmen, everyone takes a turn cleaning the toilets," he said.

"Don't forget these are all very talented people, people of great human qualities. They are intelligent and they are in professions in which they face a lot of stress," the doctor said. The Peruvian hostages were teaching the 24 Japanese Spanish, and some of the Peruvian hostages were learning Japanese, he said.
SOMETIMES THEIR SONGS CAN BE HEARD
Sometimes people outside can hear them singing together, followed by applause. Recently they were heard singing the sad Mexican ranchero "Ojos Negros" (Dark Eyes).

Red Cross staffers bring in food and hostages choose between Japanese and Peruvian meals. The only hostage who is neither Peruvian nor Japanese, Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio, was reported to have suffered some kind of emotional breakdown after a fierce argument with one of the rebels, which ended with the rebel pointing a gun at Gumucio.

Several of the hostages -- and a few of the guerrillas -- are showing signs of stress-related disorders like swollen gums, hair loss and skin diseases that cause flaking and uncontrollable itching, the doctor said. "They're showing the typical complications of chronic angst," he said.

The only hostage with real health problems is Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja, who suffers from heart and kidney disease. Red Cross staffers are delivering mediation he needs, the doctor said. "If any of the hostages were in danger of death the MRTA would allow us to evacuate him, I'm sure of it," he said. "They don't want anybody to die of disease on their watch."

Jhon Caro said that despite the Gumucio incident it was likely the hostage-takers were starting to feel some affection for their captives, as often happens in such cases. The rebels never followed through on early threats to execute hostages by lot unless the government yielded on their demand to release their more than 400 jailed comrades.
"After 90 days in isolation, you start to think differently," Jhon Caro said. "For the terrorists, their aggression and intolerance towards these people has probably been softened."
